# The Mercy of Forgetting

In 1942, Jorge Luis Borges published a story about a man who could not forget. Ireneo Funes, a young man from a dusty river town on the Uruguayan shore, is thrown from a horse and wakes with his perception sharpened to an unbearable edge. From then on he remembers everything: not just events but every leaf of every vine in the yard, seen once, held forever. He can reconstruct a whole day in his mind — though, Borges notes, it takes him a full day to do it. He sleeps badly, because to sleep is to turn one's mind from the world, and Funes cannot turn from anything. What he cannot do, Borges tells us quietly at the end, is think. "To think is to forget differences, to generalize, to abstract. In the teeming world of Funes, there were only details, almost contemporaneous details." The man who kept everything could make nothing of it. His perfect memory was not a magnified life. It was the absence of one.

Borges invented Funes, but he did not invent the condition. By the time the story appeared, a Russian neuropsychologist named Alexander Luria had already spent two decades studying a real Funes. Solomon Shereshevsky was a newspaper reporter whose editor noticed, with mounting irritation, that he never took notes. Summoned to Luria's laboratory, he listened to long strings of words and numbers and nonsense syllables and repeated them back — forward, backward, in any order requested — and could do the same with lists Luria had read him years earlier, reproducing exactly, decades on, a syllable string from a single afternoon in the 1920s. And yet the gift was closer to a haunting than a talent. Shereshevsky's memories arrived as images of almost hallucinatory vividness, every word detonating its own private scene, so that he struggled to read poetry (too many pictures), to recognize faces (expressions kept rearranging them), or to grasp even a simple idea (every abstraction was smothered beneath its instances). Tormented by the residue of trivial days, he tried to forget on purpose. He wrote things down, hoping his mind would treat the paper as a storage place and release its copies. When that failed, he burned the paper — and failed again, because he could still see the charred edges of the letters glowing against the dark. He ended up performing his wound for a living, a mnemonist on the stages of Moscow music halls.

Two men, one fictional and one real, arrived at the same discovery from opposite directions: total memory is not the summit of mind but its breakdown.

This is not how we usually talk about forgetting. Forgetting is failure, we say. "I forgot" is an apology. Entire industries exist to shore up our leaky memories — calendars, apps, supplements, games that promise to train the brain — and our deepest fear of illness is the fear of the archive eroding, the self dissolving as the record disappears. We treat memory as the essence of a person and forgetting as the essence of memory's defeat. But the cases of Funes and Shereshevsky suggest we have the anatomy upside down. Forgetting is not what happens when memory breaks. Forgetting is what allows memory to work at all. What we call remembering is, for the most part, forgetting done well.

Consider what memory actually is. It is not playback. There is no tape. When you recall your tenth birthday, you are not retrieving a stored film; you are rebuilding a scene

# The Mercy of Forgetting

In 1942, Jorge Luis Borges published a story about a man who could not forget. Ireneo Funes, a frugal teenager from a dusty town on the Uruguayan shore, is thrown from a horse and wakes with his perception sharpened to an unbearable edge. From then on he remembers everything: not just events but every leaf of every vine in the yard, seen once, held forever. He can reconstruct a whole day in his mind — though, Borges notes, it takes him a full day to do it. He has trouble sleeping, because to sleep is to turn one's mind from the world, and Funes cannot turn from anything. What he cannot do, Borges tells us quietly at the end, is think. "To think is to forget a difference, to generalize, to abstract. In the teeming world of Funes, there were only details, nearly simultaneous details." The man who kept everything could not make anything of it. His perfect memory was not a magnified life. It was the absence of one.

(~170 words)

Borges invented Funes, but he did not invent the condition. By the time the story appeared, a Russian neuropsychologist named Alexander Luria had already been studying a real Funes for twenty years. Solomon Shereshevsky was a newspaper reporter whose editor noticed, with irritation, that he never took notes. Summoned to Luria's laboratory, he was read long strings of words and numbers and nonsense syllables and repeated them back — forward, backward, in any order — and could do the same with lists Luria had read him years earlier, including, decades on, a syllable string from a single afternoon in the 1920s. And yet the gift was closer to a haunting than a talent. Shereshevsky's memories arrived as images of almost hallucinatory vividness, each word detonating its own private scene, so that he struggled to read poetry (too many pictures), to recognize faces (expressions kept changing the face), or to grasp a simple idea (every abstraction was smothered under its instances). Tormented by the residue of trivial days, he tried to forget on purpose. He wrote things down, hoping his mind would treat the paper as a storage place and release its copies. When that failed, he burned the paper — and failed again, because he could still see the charred edges of the letters glowing against the dark. He eventually made his living as a stage mnemonist, a man in a music hall performing his wound.

(~200 words)

Two men — one fictional, one real — arrived at the same discovery from opposite directions: that total memory is not the summit of mind but its breakdown. [short transition]

This is not how we usually talk about forgetting. Forgetting is failure, we say. "I forgot" is an apology. Entire industries exist to prop up our leaky memories — calendars, apps, supplements, brain-training games — and our deepest fear of illness is the fear of losing the archive, of the self dissolving as the record erodes. We treat memory as the essence of a person and forgetting as the essence of memory's defeat.

But the cases of Funes and Shereshevsky suggest we have the anatomy upside down. Forgetting is not what happens when memory breaks. Forgetting is what allows memory to work. What we call remembering is, for the most part, forgetting done well.

(~150 words)

Consider what memory actually is. It is not playback. There is no tape. When you recall your tenth birthday, you are not retrieving a stored film; you are rebuilding a scene from fragments, and each rebuilding subtly rewrites the original. The psychologist Elizabeth Loftus showed decades ago how easily the record can be edited — how a suggestive question can relocate a car crash, and how, in her most famous study, a quarter of participants could be brought to "remember" being lost in a shopping mall as a child, an event that never happened. This sounds like a scandal, evidence that the mind is defective. It is closer to evidence that the mind is doing something else entirely. The brain was never designed to be an archive. Archives are cheap now; we know what they look like, and we know what they demand. The brain is not an archive. It is an editor. It does not keep the footage. It keeps the takeaway.

(~150 words)

Hermann Ebbinghaus gave us the numbers in 1885, memorizing nonsense syllables and charting what he lost. The curve was brutal: most of what he learned was gone within a day, and within a week only crumbs remained. Every student has felt this curve as an insult. But look at it again from the standpoint of design rather than defeat, and it starts to look like triage. A mind that kept everything would be Shereshevsky's mind, and Shereshevsky could not get through a poem. The steepness of forgetting is the price of pattern. And the deepest editing happens at night. In slow-wave sleep, the brain replays the day's most important traces and lets the rest dissolve; the synapses grown during learning are scaled back; a waste-clearing system flushes the debris of cognition out like a street-cleaning crew working the empty avenues. "Sleep on it" sounds like a proverb. It is engineering advice. A night of forgetting is how a day becomes knowledge.

(~155 words)

Even Proust, that great archivist of the inner life, owed his masterpiece to forgetting. Voluntary memory, he found, gives nothing but "the memory of the intelligence" — a flat inventory, Combray as a list. It was only because the world of his childhood had been wholly lost that the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea could detonate in him and bring back the parish entire. In a world of Funeses there are no madeleines. Nothing can return suddenly, with the shock of resurrection, because nothing has ever left. Wonder requires loss. Forgetting is what gives memory its drama — not the keeping but the return.

(~110 words)

***

Michelangelo is said to have described his method simply: "I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free." Every life is such a block of stone: everything that happened, all of it, undifferentiated — every hour of every commute, every weather, every stranger's face at every window. What we call a memory — the smell of rain on one particular street, a sentence a friend said twenty years ago that still runs under certain days like a river under ice — survives not despite the rest being gone but because the rest is gone. Forgetting is the chisel. Meaning is what remains standing after the carving. And a self, it turns out, is not the stone. It is the figure the carving leaves.

(~125 words)

Nietzsche saw this with his usual ruthless clarity. It is possible, he wrote, to live almost without memory; it is altogether impossible to live without forgetting. He pointed at the cattle in the field — grazing, incurious, happy — as creatures of pure presence, and suggested that our unhappiness lies in being unable to graze, unable not to drag yesterday into every present moment. But his point becomes sharpest when we look at what happens when the chisel stops. Trauma is forgetting's failure. In post-traumatic stress, a memory refuses to be filed as the past; it returns in the present tense, at full volume, unedited raw footage forcing itself into the room. Among Daniel Schacter's "seven sins of memory," six are failures to remember well — but the seventh, persistence, is remembering too much, too well, and it is the sin that destroys lives. Therapy, at its core, is often the slow, patient work of teaching a memory that it is over. And the same mercy operates on a humbler scale, everywhere, constantly. You cannot re-feel the pain of your worst injury; you can only remember that you suffered, the way you remember a fact from a book — which is the only reason anyone has a second child. Heartbreak keeps its facts and surrenders its texture. Time does not heal, whatever the bumper stickers say. Time edits. And the editing is the healing.

(~205 words)

For most of human history, forgetting was the default and remembering the labor. Paper faded. Tapes degraded. Witnesses died. Records burned, accidentally and otherwise. Even the law knew this: the feud ended not because anyone signed a treaty but because the deed at its center had blurred beyond use. Then, in one long lifetime, the polarity flipped. Now remembering is the default, and forgetting requires effort — and usually fails. Every photograph taken is stored. Every message sent is kept. The careless thing you posted at seventeen sits in the archive, patient as a debt, waiting for the person you have since become. Social networks have built products around this: "On This Day," "Memories," a gentle notification — three years ago today — floating a photograph of a funeral over your breakfast. In 2014, the European Court of Justice ruled that a Spanish man named Mario Costeja González could demand that Google stop linking to an ancient auction notice of his repossessed home, and the world suddenly had a name for the thing he was asking for: the right to be forgotten. The phrase sounds dystopian until you sit with what its absence means.

(~180 words)

Faulkner wrote that the past is never dead, that it is not even past. He meant it as a haunting. The archive makes it literal. And a self is a strange thing to have perfectly preserved, because a self is also something that is supposed to keep changing. The person of ten years ago is, in many ways, someone you have laboriously stopped being; the archive disagrees, and the archive wins arguments by remaining. There is a subtler cost, too. When everything is quotable forever, speech becomes cautious. Not because we value discretion more, but because every sentence might be a tattoo. We begin to compose for the archive rather than for the room — performing permanence instead of living — and a culture of archival creatures may find, one day, that it has stopped saying anything worth archiving.

(~130 words)

None of this is to say that all forgetting is innocent. There is a malignant forgetting: the erasure of atrocity, the smoothed-over grave, the state that declares some people never existed. Ernest Renan, in his famous lecture on the nation, said that forgetting — "I would even go so far as to say historical error" — is essential to the creation of a nation, and he was describing a real and dangerous power. Peace between peoples often requires that grievances be allowed to blur, and justice requires that they not. So the question is never whether to forget but who holds the chisel — whether the release is chosen, a grace extended, or imposed, a theft of the past from those to whom it belonged. Forgetting, like memory, has a politics, and the difference between mercy and erasure is the difference between giving something up and taking it away.

(~135 words)

***

The hardest case is the one we fear most, and it deserves honesty rather than poetry. Dementia is not a peaceful garden where burdens are laid down; it is a catastrophe, and no essay about the uses of forgetting should pretend otherwise. And yet even there, at the ocean floor of memory, something strange surfaces. The musicologist Clive Wearing, after a viral infection destroyed his hippocampus in 1985, was left with a memory a few seconds long. His diary from those years is almost unbearable to read — page after page of entries like "Now I am truly awake," "Now I am perfectly, overwhelmingly awake," each one crossed out, the discovery of consciousness made and re-made and re-made. He cannot hold a thought from one minute to the next. But his hands remember Chopin. Given a piano, he plays — beautifully, in full — because music lives somewhere below the episodic record, in the procedural deep. And when his wife Deborah enters the room, he greets her with a joy so complete it seems to have no history, because for him it doesn't; it is first love, again and again. Deborah has written that she stopped mourning the man who was gone because the man who remained loved her no less. What remains when the story is gone? The love was never only the story. Somewhere beneath the archive there is a self that is not made of records at all — made instead of habits, melodies, gravities — and that self, it turns out, is the one we were talking about all along.

You have forgotten nearly everything that has ever happened to you. Almost none of your days survive in any form. The names of your elementary school classmates have slipped away one by one; the worries that once occupied whole seasons of your life have left no address. I no longer think of this as failure. The forgotten is not lost. It is spent — used up, the way fuel is spent, in the construction of the person who no longer needs it. Every generalization you own was bought with a thousand particulars surrendered; every abstraction, every skill, every settled belief is a pile of vanished Tuesdays compressed into something you can use. The details had to go so that the pattern could stay, the way the chiseled marble had to fall away so the angel could walk out of the stone.

# The Mercy of Forgetting

In 1942, Jorge Luis Borges published a story about a man who could not forget. Ireneo Funes, a frugal teenager from a dusty town on the Uruguayan shore, is thrown from a horse and wakes with his perception sharpened to an unbearable edge. From then on he remembers everything: not just events but every leaf of every vine in the yard, seen once, held forever. He can reconstruct a whole day in his mind — though, Borges notes, it takes him a full day to do it. He has trouble sleeping, because to sleep is to turn one's mind from the world, and Funes cannot turn from anything. What he cannot do, Borges tells us quietly at the end, is think. "To think is to forget a difference, to generalize, to abstract. In the teeming world of Funes, there were only details, nearly simultaneous details." The man who kept everything could not make anything of it. His perfect memory was not a magnified life. It was the absence of one.

(~170 words)

Borges invented Funes, but he did not invent the condition. By the time the story appeared, a Russian neuropsychologist named Alexander Luria had already been studying a real Funes for twenty years. Solomon Shereshevsky was a newspaper reporter whose editor noticed, with irritation, that he never took notes. Summoned to Luria's laboratory, he was read long strings of words and numbers and nonsense syllables and repeated them back — forward, backward, in any order — and could do the same with lists Luria had read him years earlier, including, decades on, a syllable string from a single afternoon in the 1920s. And yet the gift was closer to a haunting than a talent. Shereshevsky's memories arrived as images of almost hallucinatory vividness, each word detonating its own private scene, so that he struggled to read poetry (too many pictures), to recognize faces (expressions kept changing the face), or to grasp a simple idea (every abstraction was smothered under its instances). Tormented by the residue of trivial days, he tried to forget on purpose. He wrote things down, hoping his mind would treat the paper as a storage place and release its copies. When that failed, he burned the paper — and failed again, because he could still see the charred edges of the letters glowing against the dark. He eventually made his living as a stage mnemonist, a man in a music hall performing his wound.

(~200 words)

Two men — one fictional, one real — arrived at the same discovery from opposite directions: that total memory is not the summit of mind but its breakdown. [short transition]

This is not how we usually talk about forgetting. Forgetting is failure, we say. "I forgot" is an apology. Entire industries exist to prop up our leaky memories — calendars, apps, supplements, brain-training games — and our deepest fear of illness is the fear of losing the archive, of the self dissolving as the record erodes. We treat memory as the essence of a person and forgetting as the essence of memory's defeat.

But the cases of Funes and Shereshevsky suggest we have the anatomy upside down. Forgetting is not what happens when memory breaks. Forgetting is what allows memory to work. What we call remembering is, for the most part, forgetting done well.

(~150 words)

Consider what memory actually is. It is not playback. There is no tape. When you recall your tenth birthday, you are not retrieving a stored film; you are rebuilding a scene from fragments, and each rebuilding subtly rewrites the original. The psychologist Elizabeth Loftus showed decades ago how easily the record can be edited — how a suggestive question can relocate a car crash, and how, in her most famous study, a quarter of participants could be brought to "remember" being lost in a shopping mall as a child, an event that never happened. This sounds like a scandal, evidence that the mind is defective. It is closer to evidence that the mind is doing something else entirely. The brain was never designed to be an archive. Archives are cheap now; we know what they look like, and we know what they demand. The brain is not an archive. It is an editor. It does not keep the footage. It keeps the takeaway.

(~150 words)

Hermann Ebbinghaus gave us the numbers in 1885, memorizing nonsense syllables and charting what he lost. The curve was brutal: most of what he learned was gone within a day, and within a week only crumbs remained. Every student has felt this curve as an insult. A mind that kept everything would be Shereshevsky's mind, and Shereshevsky could not get through a poem. The steepness of forgetting is the price of pattern. And the deepest editing happens at night. In slow-wave sleep, the brain replays the day's most important traces and lets the rest dissolve; the synapses grown during learning are scaled back; a waste-clearing system flushes the debris of cognition out like a street-cleaning crew working the empty avenues. (~155 words)

Even Proust, that great archivist of the inner life, owed his masterpiece to forgetting. Voluntary memory, he found, gives nothing but "the memory of the intelligence" — a flat inventory, Combray as a list. It was only because the world of his childhood had been wholly lost that the taste of a madeleine dipped in tea could detonate in him and bring back the parish entire. Forgetting is what gives memory its drama — not the keeping but the return.

Michelangelo is said to have described his method simply: "I saw the angel in the marble and carved until I set him free." Every life is such a block of stone: everything that happened, all of it, undifferentiated — every hour of every commute, every weather, every stranger's face at every window. What we call a memory — the smell of rain on one particular street, a sentence a friend said twenty years ago that still runs under certain days like a river under ice — survives not despite the rest being gone but because the rest is gone. Forgetting is the chisel. Meaning is what remains standing after the carving. And a self, it turns out, is not the stone. It is the figure the carving leaves.

(~125 words)

Nietzsche saw this with his usual ruthless clarity. It is possible, he wrote, to live almost without memory; it is altogether impossible to live without forgetting. He pointed at the cattle in the field — grazing, incurious, happy — as creatures of pure presence, and suggested that our unhappiness lies in being unable to graze, unable not to drag yesterday into every present moment. But his point becomes sharpest when we look at what happens when the chisel stops. Trauma is forgetting's failure. In post-traumatic stress, a memory refuses to be filed as the past; it returns in the present tense, at full volume, unedited raw footage forcing itself into the room. For most of human history, forgetting was the default and remembering the labor. Paper faded. Tapes degraded. Witnesses died. Records burned, accidentally and otherwise. Now remembering is the default, and forgetting requires effort — and usually fails. Every photograph taken is stored. Every message sent is kept. The careless thing you posted at seventeen sits in the archive, patient as a debt, waiting for the person you have since become. Social networks have built products around this: "On This Day," "Memories," a gentle notification — three years ago today — floating a photograph of a funeral over your breakfast. The phrase sounds dystopian until you sit with what its absence means.

Faulkner wrote that the past is never dead, that it is not even past. He meant it as a haunting. The archive makes it literal. And a self is a strange thing to have perfectly preserved, because a self is also something that is supposed to keep changing. We begin to compose for the archive rather than for the room — performing permanence instead of living — and a culture of archival creatures may find, one day, that it has stopped saying anything worth archiving.

None of this is to say that all forgetting is innocent. There is a malignant forgetting: the erasure of atrocity, the smoothed-over grave, the state that declares some people never existed. Ernest Renan, in his famous lecture on the nation, said that forgetting — "I would even go so far as to say historical error" — is essential to the creation of a nation, and he was describing a real and dangerous power. Peace between peoples often requires that grievances be allowed to blur, and justice requires that they not. The hardest case is the one we fear most, and it deserves honesty rather than poetry. Dementia is not a peaceful garden where burdens are laid down; it is a catastrophe, and no essay about the uses of forgetting should pretend otherwise. And yet even there, at the ocean floor of memory, something strange surfaces. The musicologist Clive Wearing, after a viral infection destroyed his hippocampus in 1985, was left with a memory a few seconds long.
